Basic Architecture (GameObjects)

GameObjects and Components:
Base GameObject has name, tag, layer, and transform component
Scripts Are Components and define the empty GameObject
GameObjects are Initialised and run when play is pressed 

Scripts must be attached to a GameObject in order for scripts to run.
Scripts can be attached to an Empty gameObject.

All GameObjects Components and Scripts in scene(s) in build
Are available to run if accessed and visible. 

GameObjects will have variable and references that can be modified.
References can be to any Components, GameObjects, or Assets.

Could create all elements from empty GameObject if desired.
https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-GameObject.html

Unity is initialised and run from the Main Camera object.
This is the minimum requirement in order to build and run a scene/level

Basic Architecture (Components)

Components are scripts, either pre-defined library or user defined

GameObjects will come with default Components depending on 
Type, and these define the blank GameObject.

The Transform Component is the basic GameObject Component, 
Along with name, tag, and layer.

Basic Architecture (Inspector Window)

GameObjects, Scripts, and other assets are available for review and change in the Inspector Window. This exposes the individual components attached. You can add, remove, toggle active mode, or change and add/subtract parameters that are exposed. 

Public script variables declared are exposed here for value input or links to other game objects by drag and drop.

References to data files or other GameObjects may be exposed by the script and available here.

Components are added at the bottom.

Basic Architecture (Inspector Window)

Some default and possible library/added components include:
Name
Visibility – Turns object on and off. Simple.
Static – Game information Precomputed for non moving object – not same as for variables and methods
Tag – Allows naming for scripts to access (Collisions)
Layer – Cameras, Lights, can render certain layers, Raycasting can ignore
	(Camera Culling Mask, Raycast Layermask)
Transform – translation, rotation, scaling
Renderer – displays object
MeshRenderer – has rendering options, materials
Collider

Object-­‐oriented programming (OOP) is a programming language model organized around "objects" rather than "actions" and data rather than logic. Historically, a program has been viewed as a logical procedure that takes input data, processes it, and produces output data.

OOP Concepts

Encapsulation

Abstraction

OOP Concepts

Encapsulation: 

Bundling Data(attributes) and Methods(Functions) operating on the data into a single unit (class). 

This hides (protects) internal state and requires interaction performed through and objects methods.

OOP Concepts

Abstraction:

Hiding complex implementation and only showing essential features of objects.

This reduces complexity and isolates change impacts.

OOP Concepts

Inheritance:

A class can inherit attributes from another class. (parent/child, super/sub)

This promotes code reuse and establishes class relationships.

OOP Concepts

Polymorphism:

Using a common interface for multiple data types.

Different classes can be treated as instances of the same class through a shared interface.

Classes:
The first step in OOP is to identify all the objects you want to manipulate and how they relate to each other, an exercise often known as data modeling. Once you've identified an object, you generalize it as a class of objects and define the kind of data it contains and any logic sequences that can manipulate it. Each distinct logic sequence is known as a method. A real instance of a class is called an “object” or an “instance of a class”. The object or class instance is what you run in the computer. Its methods provide computer instructions and the class object characteristics provide relevant data. You communicate with objects -­‐ and they communicate with each other.

Working in Unity (C# and OOP Concepts)

Each script that you create will by default inherit from MonoBehaviour. We will discuss this class at a later point. Each script that you create will also have two functions defined by default: Start() and Update().
The Start() function will be run only once at the start of the program. So any logic and data initializations that you need or want to do can be placed in the Start() function.
The Update() function is where most of the magic happens. This is the function that gets called continuously throughout the life of your game or simulation. This is the function where you will update your game objects. In short it is the function which will be called each frame before rendering the scene.

Classes:

Everything in C# is based on Classes. Classes are declared by using the keyword class followed by the class name and a set of class members surrounded by curly braces.   A class normally consists of Methods, Fields and Properties. Every class has a constructor, which is called automatically any time an instance of a class is created. The purpose of constructors is to initialize class members when an instance of the class is created. Constructors do not have return values and always have the same name as the class. Unity handles the constuctor for you in a Game Object.

Declaring - Declaring a variable means to introduce a new variable to the program. You define its type and its name.
	int a; //a is declared

Instantiate - Instantiating a class means to create a new instance of the class. 
	MyObject x = new MyObject(); //we are making a new instance of the class MyObject

Initialize - To initialize a variable means to assign it an initial value.
	int a; //a is declared	int a = 0; //a is declared AND initialized to 0	MyObject x = new MyObject(); //x is declared and initialized with an instance of MyObject

Assigning - Assigning to a variable means to provide the variable with a value.

Unity (C#) (GameObjects)

GameObjects are the fundamental objects in Unity that represent characters, props, and scenery.They do not accomplish much in themselves, but they act as containers for Components, which implement the real functionality.

In comparison to basic C#, the GameObjects use Awake or Start instead of Constructors to initialize values. 

Unity invokes the Constructor either by the script being attached to an active game object, or at runtime by the Instantiate command on a prefab or inactive GameObject.http://answers.unity3d.com/questions/32413/using-constructors-in-unity-c.html

Unity (C#) (GameObjects)

GameObjects are the fundamental objects in Unity that represent characters, props, and scenery.They do not accomplish much in themselves, but they act as containers for Components (Scripts), which implement the real functionality.

In comparison to basic C#, the GameObjects host scripts that are derived from monobehaviour classes. These scripts are the Unity classes. the GameObjects with scripts (classes) use Awake or Start instead of Constructors to initialize values. 

Unity invokes the Awake or Start either by the script being attached to an active game object, or at runtime by the Instantiate command on a prefab or inactive GameObject.http://answers.unity3d.com/questions/32413/using-constructors-in-unity-c.html

Unity (C#) C# Basic Script

Constructor  The purpose of constructors is to initialize class members when an instance of the class is created. In Unity this is derived from MonoBehaviour

Awake  called automatically when a script is run. Called before Start. Used for references between scripts and initialisation.

Start  called automatically when a script is run. Called after Start but before Update only once script is enabled. (delay initialisation code).

Update Called once per frame per script. Frame is the PC processor time  for 1 cycle

Unity (C#) C# Basic Script
Monobehaviour classes are the basis for scripts in Unity - derived

Constructor Intitialization (generally not used in Unity)
The purpose of constructors is to initialize class members when an instance of the class is created. In Unity this is derived from MonoBehaviour. You should not use traditional C# constructors for initialization. Instead, Unity uses specific lifecycle methods like Awake(), Start(), Update(), etc.
Constructor Instantiation (generally not used in Unity)
Unity manages MonoBehaviour object instantiation internally, so the use of "new MyClass()" is rare and often inappropriate. Unity invokes the Awake or Start either by the script being attached to an active game object, or at runtime by the Instantiate command on a prefab or inactive GameObject.
Instead of constructors, use 
Awake() for initialization logic that needs to happen right when the script is loaded. called automatically when a script is run. Called before Start. Used for references between scripts and initialisation.
Start() for logic that should happen once the scene is ready. called automatically when a script is run. Called after Start but before Update only once script is enabled. (delay initialisation code).
Update() is called once per frame per script. Frame is the PC processor time  for 1 cycle.

If Statement:

The if statement is probably the most used mechanism to control the flow in your application. 
An if statement allows you to take different paths of logic, depending on a given condition. When the condition evaluates to a boolean true, a block of code for that true condition will execute. You have the option of a single if statement, multiple else if statements, and an optional else statement.

Static:
•Static is a keyword.
•You've seen it in front of Main (C# VS program files).
•If it's not there the program won't run.
•So what is static?
•To better understand what it means let's think about its opposite: dynamic.
•Dynamic is not a keyword, but dynamic means changing.
•Therefore static means it does not change.
•Static means it cannot be more than it is.
•It cannot be an object, it cannot have multiple instances .
•Static means it belongs to the class as opposed to the object (the copy of the class we create using the new keyword).
•Unless you specifically call for something to be static, it will be instance (or dynamic).
